extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112 (and pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112) for each claim, including treatment of means-plus-function claims, single-species vs genus claims, and considerations specific to chemical/biotech inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is an essential part of the examination process. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire claim must be considered, including preamble language and the transitional phrase. The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble (see Bell Communications Research; Corning Glass Works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of transitional phrases (comprising / consisting essentially of / consisting of)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional term 'comprising' is open-ended (covers recited subject matter alone or in combination with unrecited matter). 'Consisting essentially of' is a middle ground and 'consisting of' is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By using 'consisting essentially of' a drafter signals openness only to unlisted ingredients that do not materially affect the basic and novel properties; absent a clear indication in the specification or claims of what the basic and novel characteristics actually are, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' for 35 U.S.C. 102/103 purposes (see PPG). If applicant contends exclusion, applicant bears burden of showing introduction of additional steps/components would materially change characteristics (In re De Lajarte).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While examining support, the absence of definitions or details for well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The preamble's import must be determined by reviewing the entirety of the application to understand what inventors intended to encompass (Pac-Tec; Corning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the entire application to evaluate support for claimed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to determining whether the disclosure satisfies the written description requirement, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification, including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for claimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review should be from the standpoint of one of skill in the art at filing and include a determination of the field of invention and level of skill. For some arts, there is an inverse correlation between level of skill and the specificity of disclosure necessary (see Wang Labs.; Hybritech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether disclosure shows possession of the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine whether there is sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by many means (reduction to practice, detailed drawings, structural chemical formulas, or other identifying characteristics). The inquiry is factual and case-by-case (Purdue Pharma; Pfaff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention (constructing an embodiment or performing a process that meets all claim limitations and determining it works for intended purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice ordinarily provides strong evidence an invention is complete, but is not necessary in every case. For biological materials, a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may evidence reduction to practice (Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder; Mahurkar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by drawings or structural chemical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed may show possession of the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings alone can provide a 'written description' (Vas-Cath; Wolfensperger; Autogiro). In chemical claims, generic formulae may indicate what the generic claims encompass and be adequate to describe a claimed genus (Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by identifying characteristics (structure, properties, function+correlation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed relevant identifying characteristics—complete or partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics when coupled with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure—can evidence possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the art has established a strong structure-function correlation, one skilled in the art might predict structure from a function recitation. Thus written description may be satisfied through disclosure of function and minimal structure in such cases (Enzo Biochem; Falkner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only definitions are generally insufficient absent well-established correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition by function alone does not suffice to describe certain inventions (e.g., coding sequences) because it indicates what the gene does rather than what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a well-established structure-function correlation, mere recitation of function is little more than a wish or plan and does not satisfy the written description requirement (Eli Lilly; In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotech-specific identifying characteristics/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: For biomolecules, examples of identifying characteristics that may demonstrate possession include a sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, and length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of an antigen fully characterized may provide adequate written description for antibodies claimed by binding affinity if generating the antibody was routine; but if the generation was not possible by conventional technology, antibody claims may lack adequate description (Centocor; Noelle; Falkner; Capon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical invention specificity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition—structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties—not merely a wish or plan for obtaining the chemical invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to chemicals require defining features that distinguish the chemical and describe how to obtain it (Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claim (35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre-AIA 112, para. 6) support standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In considering whether there is 35 U.S.C. 112(a) support for a means-plus-function limitation, examiner must consider original disclosure in summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Adequacy is met if (1) the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform the function, or (2) it is clear one skilled in the art would have known what structure/materials/acts disclosed perform the function (see Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino). Note: relying solely on what one skilled in the art could implement is not enough to excuse inadequate disclosure in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness of means-plus-function can trigger written description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When a means-plus-function limitation is indefinite due to lack of corresponding structure/materials/acts, then the claim limitation necessarily lacks an adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) for no corresponding structure should also be accompanied by a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent disclosure of conventional/well-known information is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: What is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be disclosed in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written description requirement is applied in the context of the particular invention and state of knowledge; as fields evolve, the balance between known information and what must be disclosed shifts (Hybritech; Capon). If a skilled artisan would have understood the inventor to be in possession despite missing nuances, the requirement is met (Vas-Cath; Martin v. Johnson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus vs species analysis for claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is analyzed as a claim to that single embodiment; a claim that encompasses two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 806.04(e). The written description inquiry varies with whether the claim is to a species or genus and the nature of the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for claims drawn to a single embodiment or species
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment/species: (A) determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether the invention is complete as evidenced by drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, determine whether the invention is set forth in terms of distinguishing identifying characteristics evidenced by other descriptions sufficiently detailed to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up steps: (1) Determine if application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole—complete structure typically satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a). (2) If complete structure not disclosed, determine whether other relevant identifying characteristics are disclosed in sufficient detail so a skilled artisan would recognize possession, e.g., in biotech a strong structure-function correlation may allow function+minimal structure to suffice. If disclosure is only goals or results to be achieved, it is insufficient (In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining sufficiency of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination is factual and multifactorial: consider level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with known correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill to conclude applicant was in possession is sufficient (Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity and predictability of the art influences required disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: In mature technologies where knowledge and skill are high, written description questions should not ordinarily be raised for claims present in the original filing even if the specification discloses only a method of making and the function. In emerging and unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patents and printed publications in the art to determine whether the art is mature and what level of disclosure is necessary. In unpredictable fields, disclosure of only method and function may not support a product claim other than product-by-process (Fiers; Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, the written description requirement for a product-by-process claim is clearly satisfied; however, requirement may not be satisfied where it is not clear the acts set forth can be performed or that the product is produced by that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If process steps are not shown to be performable or don't actually produce the product, the product claim may lack written description (Amgen; Fiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and prior art to assess level of skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature and what the level of knowledge and skill is in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This informs how much detail is required in the specification to show possession; mature arts may require less explicit disclosure of well-known techniques or elements (see discussion of field maturity and Hybritech).
